transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sara (CTO, Halo), Ben (Head of ML), Evelyn (Platform), Marco (Security)

Summary:
This was a 45-60 minute product walkthrough focused on multi-tenant rate controls: we demoed a concept we labeled 'shared-rate-lanes' (a way to partition burst capacity across project tokens), showed the Console rate policy UI, and walked through Optimize suggestions (batching + KV caching). Customer asked specific questions about data residency, KMS encryption, and audit logs. We agreed to run a short pilot and exchange traffic patterns and pricing. Transcription is a bit rough in spots; some acronyms mis-heard.

[00:00] Maya: Okay hi everybody, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood Inference, um I think we have, we should have everyone, hi Sara, hi Ben, hi Evelyn, Marco, thanks for taking the time.
[00:12] Sara: Hey Maya, thanks. Super excited to see the rate controls, we've been wrestling with per-team quotas and how to let research burst without impacting production.
[00:20] Maya: Totally. Liam and Priya are here to walk through the console and the routing/guardrail setup, we'll also show how Optimize surfaces batching suggestions.
[00:30] Liam: Quick note - I'll demo two patterns: org-wide caps with project tokens for teams, and the "shared-rate-lanes" idea which gives you a pooled burst reserve. It's basically a bucket allocation that projects can tap into.
[00:45] Ben: Pooled burst reserve, okay, that sounds promising. We want dev teams to be able to run big evals without blowing prod limits.
[00:52] Evelyn: And we need the security controls: can we tie audit logs and KMS into the dedicated keys? Marco's on for that.

[01:05] Marco: Yup, main question is encryption-at-rest and customer-managed keys, and whether logs show token-level actor.
[01:12] Priya: Short answer - yes; Private and Dedicated both support CMK integrations and audit trails. Hosted has enhanced logs we can push to your SIEM. We'll show the audit view in a sec.

[01:30] Demo start - Console walkthrough
[01:32] Liam: Here is the Console. On the left you have Organizations -> Projects -> API tokens. So you can create project tokens per team.
[01:45] [02:00] Liam: If you open a token, you get policy rules: concurrency limit, token QPS, and quota windows. You can also attach it to a "lane" - we call them capacity lanes in the UI.
[02:14] Sara: Lane? Is that like a routing pool?
[02:18] Liam: Exactly. It's a routing pool with associated capacity reservations. For example you could have a Production lane with reserved GPUs and a Research lane that shares burst capacity up to X.
[02:32] Ben: How do you enforce fair share when multiple projects hit the same lane?
[02:37] Liam: We have a configurable fairshare allocator - it's proportional by project weight but you can pin sticky routing to favorites so important services maintain baseline. Also we support leaky-bucket windows per token.
[02:50] Mara (folded mislabel): [crosstalk] I mean, sorry -
[02:55] Maya: (laughs) speaker labels may move around in the transcript, apologies.

[03:05] [03:15] Liam: Now I'll show a use case - create an Org cap of 1M tokens/day, allocate project tokens A, B with base quotas, then create a shared-rate-lane with 200k tokens reserved for bursts. If A exceeds base quota it can draw from lane subject to fairshare.
[03:36] Evelyn: If A draws from the lane, does billing reflect that distinct? We need to map costs to teams.
[03:42] Priya: Good question - every token usage is attributed and you can slice billing per project token; lane usage shows up as a separate line item in the console billing export.

[04:00] [04:15] Ben: Performance - when a token draws from the burst lane, is there any latency penalty? We can't have higher p95.
[04:22] Liam: In most cases, no. The runtime routes to the same serving clusters. The only potential is when a fallback model variant is used to reduce cost - you can opt out of fallbacks for specific tokens.
[04:35] Ben: Great.

[04:45] [05:05] Demo - Optimize suggestions
[05:07] Liam: Next, Optimize. It analyzes token distributions and sequence lengths and suggests batching and KV caching profiles. For instance, it recommended a 12-16 token prefix cache for your prompt shapes, which reduced net tokens in our test by ~18%.
[05:30] Sara: How does Optimize recommend quantization? We're sensitive to quality drop.
[05:36] Priya: It gives model-specific guidance, e.g., float16 vs 4-bit quant, and shows an expected quality delta. We tie that to your eval prompt set so you can see exact regressions.

[05:50] [06:05] Security & compliance questions
[06:10] Marco: Are audit logs immutable? We need append-only with retention controls.
[06:15] Maya: Yes, audit logs are append-only. For Private/Dedicated you can ship logs to your S3 or SIEM and set retention via your bucket policies. Hosted exposes the same events and retention options as an enterprise add-on.
[06:30] Marco: SSO - we use SAML and SCIM; can you integrate with our IdP for RBAC?
[06:35] Priya: Absolutely, SAML + SCIM are supported, and Console RBAC lets you define role templates per org or project.

[06:50] [07:10] Sara: What about data residency? Some workloads must stay in eu-west.
[07:15] Maya: You can pin model serving region per org/project. Private deployments can be hosted on-prem in your EU cluster. For Hosted we have regional endpoints in EU and NA.

[07:30] [07:45] Pricing and Dedicated capacity questions
[07:47] Ben: If we go dedicated for production, how do you handle burst lane? Will research still burst?
[07:54] Liam: In Dedicated you can reserve baseline capacity and attach a burst pool that is either shared across org or limited to projects. There's an SLA-backed baseline and a best-effort burst; we can add prioritized lanes if you purchase higher tiers.
[08:10] Sara: Is the burst pool metered differently?
[08:15] Priya: Yes, metered separately; you can set soft caps and hard caps and get alerting.

[08:30] [08:45] Technical deep dive - routing behavior
[08:48] Liam: Under the hood our smart-router evaluates: token policy, lane weights, region locality, and current utilization. If a lane is saturated it will route to a fallback model variant or to another region if permitted by the policy.
[09:05] Ben: Fallback model variant — is that, like, smaller model to save cost?
[09:09] Liam: Exactly. For example you might fallback from rdx-large to rdx-medium which is faster/cheaper. You control which tokens can use fallbacks in the token policy.

[09:30] [09:45] Question from Sara: We have long inference sequences for summarization - how does KV cache play with shared lanes?
[09:52] Liam: KV cache is per model worker and per conversation. Prefix caching reduces tokens sent upstream. Lane usage is orthogonal - it's purely capacity accounting. So caching can reduce consumption of the lane.

[10:10] [10:25] Priya: Also worth noting, Optimize suggests cache TTLs and batching windows, and you can turn them on via the console or via the API.

[10:40] [11:00] Transcript artifacts and imperfections: "k-v cash" or "k v cashier" appear in the transcript occasionally and some product names were mis-typed.

[11:15] [11:30] Live scenario: Demo creating a project token and lane binding
[11:32] Liam: I'll create project token 'research-eval'. Base quota 100k/day and attach to shared lane 'research-lane' with 200k burst.
[11:45] [12:00] Liam: Now generate some synthetic load from the Console test runner - it will simulate concurrent requests.
[12:10] Ben: Watching the dashboard - I can see token-level spikes and lane consumption meter tick up. Nice.

[12:30] [12:45] Evelyn: Can we disable fallbacks for production tokens?
[12:50] Liam: Yes, set the policy flag "no_fallback" on that token.

[13:05] [13:30] Cost attribution demo
[13:32] Priya: Here's the billing export. Every event includes org_id, project_token, lane_id, model_variant, and cost columns. You can export to CSV or GCP/AWS billing integration.
[13:50] Marco: We need line items to reconcile to our internal chargeback. Good.

[14:05] [14:20] SLA and reliability
[14:22] Maya: For Dedicated we offer 99.95% uptime and latency SLOs; we also have automatic fallback policies - e.g., if a region hits 95% utilization we can route to a warm standby.
[14:38] Sara: How fast is autoscaling for burst?
[14:42] Liam: Autoscaling scales GPU pools in minutes for warm capacity; for cold starts it can be longer. So we recommend a small baseline and a burst pool for predictable spikes.

[15:00] [15:20] Integration details and APIs
[15:25] Liam: All of this is available via the Redwood REST API. Example: create token -> attach policy -> link to lane. We also provide SDKs in Python/Node.
[15:40] Ben: Can we have project tokens rotate automatically? We want short-lived tokens for CI jobs.
[15:45] Priya: We support rotating tokens, TTLs, and ephemeral tokens for CI.

[16:00] [16:15] Edge cases and limits
[16:18] Sara: If a project tries to open 1000 concurrent websockets, do you have protections?
[16:24] Liam: Yes, concurrency caps per token and per project, and global per-org caps. There's also an API rate guard to prevent abuse.

[16:40] [16:55] Customer scenario - compliance-sensitive pipeline
[16:58] Marco: For PHI data we need more controls and on-prem is likely. How does Private deployment licensing work?
[17:05] Maya: Private is licensed per cluster; you get a control plane that can run in your VPC with HSM/KMS integration. We can do an on-prem appliance for air-gapped setups.
[17:20] Marco: Log forwarding to our SIEM is supported?
[17:24] Priya: Yes - we've done Splunk/Datadog/Elastic integrations and direct S3+Glue for long-term retention.

[17:40] [17:55] Pilot discussion
[17:57] Maya: Proposed pilot: two-week trial with a dedicated test key, one research project and one production-sim project. We'll set base quotas and a shared-rate-lane and run throughput/latency tests.
[18:12] Sara: Sounds good. We'll share the token shapes and sample prompts.
[18:16] Ben: We'll also want the latency traces so we can correlate with our app metrics.

[18:30] [18:45] Questions about throttling policies
[18:48] Evelyn: If a token hits its hard cap will requests queue or fail?
[18:54] Liam: We return a 429 with a Retry-After header on hard caps. For softer caps you can queue with backpressure for short windows.

[19:10] [19:25] Pricing nuance - reserved vs metered burst
[19:28] Priya: You can reserve capacity (committed) for a lower unit cost, and have a metered burst pool at variable rates. For finance we can model different mixes.

[19:45] [20:00] Misc - obfuscations in transcript: "sticky lanes" sometimes shows as "sticky lanes" or "sticky lines" in the auto transcript.

[20:15] [20:30] Wrap-up and recap
[20:32] Maya: Quick recap - we'll set up the pilot key, Redwood to run two perf tests, Halo to send traffic patterns and CSV of token usage, Redwood to share SOC2 docs and private deployment sheet. Anything to add?
[20:50] Sara: Also please include a sample billing export so we can see the line items.
[20:55] Maya: Noted. 
[21:05] Ben: Can we have an optional deep dive on fallback behavior next week with your infra team?
[21:10] Liam: Yes, we can schedule a technical deep dive.

[21:20] [21:30] Closing
[21:32] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the next steps and the pilot setup.
[21:40] Sara: Thanks, bye.
